\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped---a dichotomy with a mechanistic basis.
Under nucleus sampling, top-$p$ truncation preserves the functional form of the conditional distribution at each step; what changes is the \emph{input}: as the model conditions on increasingly self-typical outputs, expected NLL compresses monotonically.
This yields two testable predictions: (1)~increasing sampling randomness should weaken the location drift, and (2)~semantic-preservation constraints should attenuate it.
Both are confirmed: at $t{=}1.0$, location signal collapses ($\rho$: $-0.60 \to -0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}); under elaboration prompts, drift weakens (F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
Causal analyses corroborate: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification, with 6/7 exhibiting significant Granger causality (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).

The classifier is a proof-of-concept for corpus-level auditing, not per-document filtering: gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for individual flagging but supports batch-level contamination estimation (${\pm}3$--$4$\% at $n{=}1{,}000$; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Depth-aware filtering can serve as a prophylactic against model collapse \cite{drayson_detection_prevents_collapse}, though depth-stratified curation does not yet improve downstream training (TOST equivalence at $\varepsilon{=}{\pm}2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
The primary value thus lies in data provenance---determining recursive rewriting depth---rather than training improvement.

DDR is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: retraining erodes tail coverage by updating weights, whereas inference-chain drift at fixed parameters shifts only location, leaving shape stable.
Vocabulary impoverishment alone cannot explain this asymmetry: if depth simplified the lexicon, shape features should also compress, yet they remain stable ($d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Prior work documents \emph{what converges}---diversity loss \cite{curious_decline}, attractor dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}---but not what is \emph{preserved}; this complementary observation enables depth detection without per-generator calibration.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA recovers more signal (F1\,=\,0.905, 6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), reflecting token-order patterns that aggregate statistics miss.
Instruction-tuned models show compressed fingerprints (DDR silhouette 0.660$\to$0.372; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), though QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91, suggesting depth signal persists at the token-sequence level beyond DDR's feature decomposition.

\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
\label{tab:clustering}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
\toprule
$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
\midrule
2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\

 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\

The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.

\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

\midrule

Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.

## N2: Nucleus Sampling Confound

This is the most critical question. Let me think carefully.

The reviewer's concern: shape stability might be a trivial consequence of nucleus sampling's top-p truncation, not an interesting finding.

The paper's current Discussion (line 5) actually addresses this head-on: "Under nucleus sampling, top-p truncation preserves the functional form of the conditional distribution at each step; what changes is the input: as the model conditions on increasingly self-typical outputs, expected NLL compresses monotonically."
 
The paper only tests nucleus sampling at top-p=0.95, though there is temperature ablation across τ=0.5/0.7/0.9/1.0 where the location signal collapses at τ=1.0—but that's a different sampling strategy entirely. The core tension is whether shape stability under nucleus sampling is a trivial artifact of the truncation mechanism itself, or whether it reveals something meaningful about the model's behavior. On one hand, nucleus sampling by definition preserves relative probability proportions within the truncated set, so some degree of shape preservation seems mechanically expected. On the other hand, the specific pattern of flat tail decay and the monotonic NLL compression as the model self-conditions suggests something more than just truncation mechanics at play.

The evidence leans toward this being informative rather than trivial. The input distribution shifts at each generation step as the model becomes increasingly self-typical, so even under nucleus sampling the conditional distribution shape could plausibly change—yet it doesn't. Temperature scaling at 0.9 compresses effect sizes while preserving the hierarchy, which isn't explained by truncation alone. The fact that location drifts while shape remains stable is itself the key finding explaining why cross-generator detection works. Model collapse literature shows tail erosion under recursive generation, demonstrating that shape can degrade under these conditions. And greedy decoding would eliminate stochasticity entirely, making features constant—which actually supports the argument that some randomness is necessary for the signal to persist.

So R2's skepticism has some validity but overstates the concern. Shape stability under nucleus sampling isn't trivially expected because the input distribution genuinely changes at each step, and the question of whether the conditional distribution shape tracks those changes is empirically interesting. The paper should probably acknowledge this more explicitly and perhaps test alternative sampling strategies to strengthen the claim.

Running greedy and top-k experiments would be compelling evidence, though risky given the timeline. Greedy decoding is trivial to implement and fast, and top-k is similarly straightforward. Regenerating chains across multiple generators with different sampling strategies would take maybe 1-1.5 days of GPU time if parallelized, but there's real risk that identical results across strategies would actually weaken the paper rather than strengthen it.

Actually, the more I think about it, greedy decoding would converge to a fixed point after a few steps, making both location and shape deterministic—which wouldn't help address R2's concern at all. Top-k would likely show similar DDR to nucleus sampling since both use truncation, which would support the claim that DDR is a property of truncated sampling rather than nucleus-specific. And the paper already has full sampling at temperature 1.0, which collapses the location signal entirely. So the real question is whether these additional experiments actually clarify the mechanism or just add noise to the narrative.

I'm leaning toward Option B—it's the safer, more honest approach. The temperature experiment at τ=1.0 already gives us the key empirical point, and running new experiments at the deadline is risky if the results don't cleanly support the story. The decomposition itself (location versus shape) is genuinely novel regardless of whether DDR is nucleus-specific, and the model collapse literature already suggests that shape erosion under retraining is distinct from what happens during inference. I should strengthen this framing with a more specific mechanistic argument about why the inference chain stability matters.

Now I'm thinking through the statistical framework details. The tail_decay labeling should probably be "boundary" rather than "weakly responsive"—it's more precise given the TOST pass rates. The robustness check across ε∈[0.10,0.75] is reassuring—the 3/1/3 partition holds stable, which validates the choice. The convergence across multiple validation approaches is strong enough that adding gap statistic or prediction strength would be defensive overkill—the exhaustive enumeration rank, permutation test, and generator-split consistency already make the case. ## 二、N2 核心分歧：Nucleus Sampling Confound

**为什么 shape stability 不是 trivially expected：**
- Nucleus sampling 保持的是截断后分布的 *functional form*，但每一步的 *input context* 在变化（越来越 self-typical）。如果 shape stability 是 trivial 的，那 location drift 也应该被抑制——但事实上 location drift 很强（d=0.76-1.17）。说明输入变化确实影响了条件分布，只是选择性地影响了 location 而非 shape。
- Model collapse 文献（Shumailov et al., 2024）证明递归生成 CAN 侵蚀 shape（tail coverage），只是在 retraining 路径下。推理链不侵蚀 shape 是一个需要解释的实证事实，不是 trivial 推论。
- 温度实验已提供关键数据点：τ=1.0 下 location signal 崩溃（ρ: -0.60 → -0.002），但 appendix_temperature_stability.tex 显示 near-stationary 特征在所有温度下保持 d<0.15。这说明 shape stability 不仅是 nucleus 特定的——它在全采样（full sampling）下也成立。

**但论文确实缺的是**：greedy decoding 这个极端对照。greedy 下链会快速收敛到固定点（deterministic），所有特征都稳定——这不是 DDR，是 trivial convergence。如果有这个数据，就能画出完整谱系：greedy（无 DDR）→ low-temp nucleus（强 DDR）→ high-temp（弱 DDR）→ full sampling（无 DDR），证明 DDR 是"有限随机性"的涌现属性。

**选项 A（DDL 前跑实验）**：
- 技术可行：greedy + top-k 只需改 `do_sample=False` / `top_k=50`，无代码难度

**选项 B（纯 framing）**：
- **这是正确策略**，但需要比你提的方案更强：
  1. **承认 limitation**："Our findings are established under nucleus sampling (p=0.95); future work should verify under alternative decoding strategies."

**能否说服 R2 从 3.0 → 3.5**：坦率说不太可能仅靠 framing。R2 要的是实验证据。但 framing 改善可以从"明显弱点"变成"acknowledged limitation"，降低被硬扣分的风险。真正的改善在 rebuttal 阶段补实验。

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

AI text detection asks a single binary question---\emph{human or machine?}---and recent methods answer it with increasing reliability \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
Yet this framing elides a richer structure emerging on the open web: as LLM outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{recursive depths}---an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and each generation cycle pushes distributional properties further from both the human source and the first-generation predecessor.
While most deployed LLM outputs use instruction-tuned models, base-model generation pipelines remain prevalent in synthetic data production, pre-training corpus construction, and recursive data augmentation; we accordingly scope this study to base (pretrained) models.
Knowing \emph{how many times} text has been recursively generated matters for data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} and model collapse analysis \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}, yet no current method moves beyond the binary boundary.

We introduce \emph{depth fingerprinting}: classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) and decomposing the distributional drift that accumulates across depths into structurally distinct components.
The core empirical finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$; convergence across parametric and non-parametric effect-size measures confirms this partition).
This location/shape asymmetry exposes a structural property of fixed-parameter autoregressive sampling: the decoding mechanism systematically compresses where the output distribution sits while preserving its higher-order form---a pattern mechanistically distinct from the tail-coverage erosion in model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, and analytically informative independent of both the specific mechanism and classification accuracy.
Concurrent work characterizes convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}; ours is the first to decompose the drift into complementary location and shape components and to leverage this asymmetry for cross-generator depth prediction.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation dynamics from alignment artifacts (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

As a proof of concept, a lightweight 7-feature ensemble informed by DDR achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, surpassing individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp; an end-to-end QLoRA classifier reaches 0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that the depth signal extends well beyond handcrafted features.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Empirical decomposition (DDR).} Clustering-based validation ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) confirms that inference-chain drift separates into a drifting location component ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and a stable shape component ($d < 0.10$). Where prior work documents \emph{what converges}---diversity loss \cite{curious_decline}, attractor dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}---DDR identifies \emph{what is preserved}: shape invariance provides the cross-generator reference needed for depth detection without per-generator calibration.
    \item \textbf{Task formulation and evaluation suite.} We define generation depth classification as an ordinal prediction task and construct a controlled dataset of 37K texts from eight generators across five families (0.6B--8B), with leave-one-generator-out cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol.
\end{enumerate}
We additionally provide a proof-of-concept classifier (binary F1\,=\,0.694) and systematically map its operating boundaries across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, and model scale, establishing where DDR-based detection succeeds and where it fails.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	The detection literature spans statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies}, zero-shot scoring \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, geometric invariants \cite{intrinsic_dim_detection}, and learned classifiers \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
8	RAID \cite{raid} benchmarks binary detection across generators and attacks; we extend the task from binary to ordinal depth estimation.
9	Several recent efforts move beyond the binary boundary---collaboration roles \cite{beyond_binary}, joint detection-attribution \cite{two_birds}, creator-editor modes \cite{beyond_final_actor}, multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}---but all taxonomize by \emph{source} or \emph{production mode}, not recursive generation \emph{depth}; repurposing their scores as depth predictors reveals high cross-generator variance (binary F1\,=\,0.52--0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
10	Our contribution is orthogonal: the task formulation itself (ordinal depth classification \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,coral_ordinal,kasa_ordinality_nlp}) and the finding that drifting and stationary features together yield consistent cross-generator performance where individual detection scores do not \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}.
11	
12	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
13	\label{sec:related-collapse}
14	
15	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad,curse_of_recursion,seddik_synthetic_data}, though data mixing mitigates collapse \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
16	These studies address \emph{training-loop} degradation where parameter updates erode tail coverage; indeed, \citet{schaeffer_collapse_position} identify eight distinct definitions of ``collapse,'' most tied to retraining dynamics.
17	We study \emph{inference chains} where parameters are fixed and only the input distribution evolves.
18	Two concurrent works are most directly relevant: \citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, documenting progressive information loss, while \citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes; \citet{attractor_cycles} provide complementary evidence that LLM outputs converge to cyclic attractor states under repeated generation.
19	We study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and offer a complementary decomposition: where these works characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs, DDR isolates \emph{what} converges (NLL location) from what is preserved (NLL shape), enabling ordinal classification without per-generator calibration.
20	The independent convergence of all three approaches on ${\sim}$3 distinguishable depth classes---via Markovian dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}, information-theoretic loss \cite{broken_telephone}, and distributional feature compression (this work)---points to a shared resolution ceiling in recursive text generation (Table~\ref{tab:iterative-comparison} in Appendix~\ref{app:iterative-comparison} provides a structured comparison).
21	
22	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
23	\label{sec:related-diversity}
24	
25	Declining lexical diversity in LLM text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment settings \cite{writing_diversity}.
26	Our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}; we repurpose them from generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the depth dimension, where their monotonic decline under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling} constitutes a drifting component of DDR.
27	
28	\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
29	\label{sec:related-provenance}
30	
31	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}; generation depth offers a complementary provenance axis.
32	Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns but degrades across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, motivating passive approaches.
33	Our NLL-based analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent} (probability-tail membership inference) but extends from binary membership to full distributional decomposition for ordinal depth.
34	\citet{koike_mia_detection} formalize this connection from the opposite direction, showing that detection scores implicitly perform membership inference, underscoring the shared statistical basis of detection and provenance.
